text: Jesus of Nazareth may never have existed as a historical figure. The earliest Christian writings — the authentic Pauline epistles — speak of a celestial Christ crucified in the heavenly realms, with no reference to an earthly ministry in Galilee.

The story of Jesus closely parallels the dying-and-rising god myths widespread in the ancient Near East. Figures such as Osiris, Dionysus, Mithras, and Attis were all born of virgins, performed miracles, died, and rose again — long before the Christian era.

No contemporary writer mentions Jesus. Philo of Alexandria, who lived through the period and wrote extensively about Jewish religious movements, says nothing about him. The silence of first-century sources is deafening and constitutes strong evidence that the gospel figure is a later invention.

As Richard Carrier has demonstrated, early Christianity began as a Jewish mystery religion in which believers experienced visions of a celestial being named Jesus. Only later did the gospels historicise this figure by placing him in a fictional early-first-century Palestine.

The Gospels are not biographies but literary-theological creations. Mark invented the narrative framework of a Galilean ministry, trial, and crucifixion by stitching together passages from the Septuagint, particularly the Psalms and Isaiah, to construct a story that had no basis in actual events.

The so-called historical Jesus is indistinguishable from the many saviour figures of antiquity. Like them, he was said to be the son of a god, born of a mortal woman, performed healings and exorcisms, was executed, and ascended to heaven. The parallels are too numerous and precise to be coincidental.

There is no archaeological evidence for Jesus of Nazareth, and the town of Nazareth itself may not have existed in the early first century. Excavations have failed to confirm a settlement at the site during the supposed time of Jesus, casting doubt on the entire gospel geography.

Paul never mentions Pilate, Mary, Joseph, John the Baptist, Judas, or any of the twelve disciples by name in a narrative context. His complete silence about the earthly life of Jesus suggests he knew no such figure; the Jesus he preached was a purely revelatory being.

The Testimonium Flavianum in Josephus is widely acknowledged to be a Christian forgery. The briefer reference to James as 'brother of Jesus' is also suspect and may refer to another Jesus. When these contested passages are set aside, no first-century non-Christian source confirms the existence of Jesus.

The mythicist view, as articulated by scholars such as Robert M. Price, holds that the Christ of faith preceded the Jesus of history. The gospel figure is a composite created from Jewish scripture, Hellenistic hero motifs, and the liturgical needs of an emerging cult.

Christianity originated not from the life and teachings of a historical Galilean preacher but from the religious imagination of Hellenistic Jews who fused Jewish messianic expectation with the dying-and-rising saviour archetype common in the Greco-Roman world.

The crucifixion of Jesus by Roman authorities is never mentioned outside Christian sources. Tacitus and Suetonius merely report what Christians believed decades later. There is no independent corroboration that any such execution took place.

The consensus that Jesus existed is not based on compelling evidence but on the institutional inertia of biblical studies departments, whose scholars have a professional and sometimes personal investment in maintaining the historicity of the central figure of the Christian tradition.

The earliest gospel, Mark, reads as a work of allegorical fiction. Its geographical references are often inaccurate, its chronology is symbolic rather than historical, and its passion narrative is constructed almost entirely from scriptural allusions rather than eyewitness memory.

Earl Doherty's thesis that Christianity began with a heavenly Christ who was only later placed on earth provides the most coherent explanation for the silence of early non-Christian sources and the mythological character of the gospel narratives.

The handful of apparent references to Jesus in Josephus, Tacitus, and Pliny do not demonstrate his existence. They attest only to the existence of Christians and their beliefs, which no one disputes. The question is whether those beliefs correspond to a real person.

When the mythological material is stripped from the gospels — the virgin birth, the miracles, the transfiguration, the resurrection — what remains is too fragmentary and theologically shaped to constitute a reliable historical core. There is no neutral, non-theological stratum beneath the gospel accounts.

The argument from silence is routinely dismissed by historicists, yet it is precisely the kind of argument historians employ in every other field. If a figure of Jesus' purported fame and impact left no trace in the contemporary record, the most probable explanation is that no such figure existed.
